Abstract
The likelihood input to a Bayesian analysis almost never exactly represents how the
data were generated, calling into question the validity of posterior inferences. We review
a variational interpretation of the Bayesian posterior as an alternative justification
for its use under model misspecification, and consider the resulting implications on
uncertainty quantification and parameter estimation. We then introduce a range of
techniques that seek to obtain generalised Bayesian inferences that account for model
misspecification.
Keywords: Generalised Bayes; Gibbs posteriors; Robustness; Sensitivity analysis; Uncer-
tainty quantification

Bayesian analyses increasingly involve high-dimensional and/or observational data, and
therefore correctly modelling how the data were generated is challenging. As the famous

Outliers, for example, are generally considered a problem with the data, but could equally
result from the model missing some component of the data. Lastly, we note that in finite
parametric Bayesian models, model misspecification is somewhat more troublesome than
prior misspecification, while the influence of the prior decreases with sample size (see e.g.
Ghosal et al. , 2000; Shen and Wasserman, 2001; Walker, 2004; Wasserman, 2014), the effect
of model misspecification generally cannot be alleviated by collecting more data.
2 Bayesian inference under model misspecification
Bernardo and Smith (1994) coined the term 𝑀 -open to capture situations where ( 1) is
used to update beliefs when the model is known to be misspecified. The clearest, and most
coherent definition, of what it means to conduct a Bayesian analysis with a misspecified
model is provided by Bissiri et al. (2016), who build upon to work of Zellner (1988); Zhang
(2006a) and Walker (2013), and is further reviewed and expanded in Knoblauch et al.
(2022). Bissiri et al. (2016) identify the posterior in ( 1) as the solution to the variational
optimisation problem
𝜋(𝜃 ∣ 𝑦) = arg min
𝑞(𝜃)∈𝒫
𝔼𝑞(𝜃) [− log 𝑝(𝑦; 𝜃)] + KLD (𝑞(𝜃)||𝜋(𝜃)) , (2)
where 𝒫 is the set of all proper probability densities for 𝜃, and KLD is the Kullback-Leibler
divergence. Unlike the definition of 𝜋(𝜃 ∣ 𝑦) in ( 1), ( 2) no longer requires the model to
be correct and instead provides 𝜋(𝜃 ∣ 𝑦) with a decision theoretic foundation. Candidates
for posterior beliefs are evaluated based on their closeness to the prior, as measured by
KLD, and closeness to the data, as measured by the negative log-likelihood or the ‘self-
information’ loss

6 Discussion
We have reviewed the variational foundations of Bayesian inference in the presence of model
misspecification and introduced a range of methods designed to robustify parameter esti-
8

mation and uncertainty quantification. At the time of writing this is a new and fast moving
field. Related literature that we have not discussed includes predictive Bayesian approaches
(Fong et al. , 2023; Holmes and Walker , 2023; Fortini and Petrone , 2023) - see Fortini and
Petrone (2025) for a review; predictive extensions to the optimisation problems in ( 2) and
(4) ( Lai and Yao , 2024; Shen et al. , 2025; McLatchie et al. , 2025); 𝑒-posteriors based on
𝑒-values ( Grünwald, 2023); and connections to PAC-Bayes ( Guedj, 2019; Alquier, 2024;
Viallard et al. , 2024).
Clearly, a better specified model would remove many of the issues discussed here, and there
exists a multitude of flexible modelling techniques which include Bayesian non-parametrics
and machine learning. However, such a model should not come at the expense of the
structure a parametric model can impose and the interpretability it can provide, or be
over-burdensome computationally. It should further be acknowledged that misspecification
cannot be ruled out even in some very complex models.
